questions.q: Why does this lesson treat an NFR that exists only in one architect's memory as functionally identical to an NFR that was never decided at all?
options: Because once that person is unavailable due to ordinary staff turnover, no one else has access to the reasoning that shaped the system, making the undocumented NFR unusable to everyone else exactly as if it had never existed
Because memory-based NFRs are always technically incorrect
Because Salesforce requires all NFRs to be stored in a specific object
Because undocumented NFRs are illegal under most compliance regulations
questions.explain: An NFR that only lives in someone's head provides no value to the rest of the organization once that person is unavailable — to everyone else, it's indistinguishable from a requirement that was never actually decided.

questions.q: What does the "Source" field in this lesson's NFR register track, and why does an NFR with no identifiable source matter?
options: The Salesforce org ID where the NFR was configured
The exact line of Apex code implementing the NFR

Where the NFR came from — a specific stakeholder, an existing SLA/contract, a regulation, or an elicitation session — and an NFR with no identifiable source is worth questioning, since it may be an unvalidated assumption
The date the NFR register was first created
questions.explain: The Source field documents where a requirement actually originated. An entry with no traceable source is a red flag — it may represent an assumption that was never actually validated with a real stakeholder or document.

questions.q: Why should a design decision record created using Lesson 9's trace pattern reference a specific NFR register ID?
options: Because Salesforce requires a unique ID for every Apex class

Because cross-referencing is what makes the register useful later — someone investigating why a decision exists can look up the NFR ID, and find its full statement, source, and approval, rather than reverse-engineering the reasoning from code alone
Because NFR IDs are required fields in Salesforce's standard Case object
Because without an ID, the NFR automatically expires after 90 days
questions.explain: Cross-referencing ties the design decision back to the specific NFR that caused it, making the reasoning findable months or years later instead of requiring someone to reverse-engineer intent from the implementation alone.

questions.q: Why does an NFR register need an owner and a trigger for revisiting it, rather than being written once at project kickoff?
options: Because Salesforce automatically deletes NFR registers older than one year
Because registers must be rewritten from scratch for every new sprint
Because an owner is only needed for compliance NFRs, not for performance or scalability NFRs
Because business requirements, regulations, and actual production volumes change over time, and a register that's never revisited goes stale exactly as fast as any other static document
questions.explain: Conditions that were accurate at launch — a performance target, a regulatory assumption, a data-volume estimate — can become outdated as the business and its environment change, so the register needs an owner and a defined trigger (a major release, an annual review, a new regulation) to stay current.

questions.q: Why is a stale, untrusted NFR register described as nearly as bad as having no register at all?
options: Because once people stop trusting the register, they stop checking it and revert to relying on tribal knowledge again — exactly the failure mode the documentation was meant to prevent
Because a stale register takes up more storage space than no register
Because Salesforce treats a stale register as a security vulnerability
Because a stale register automatically fails every compliance audit
questions.explain: The whole point of a register is to replace tribal knowledge with something reliable and checkable. Once people stop trusting it because it's known to be out of date, they stop consulting it, which recreates the exact problem documentation was supposed to solve.
